Question 1

View the data for each of the 4 regression functions f1, … , f4 .

library(KernSmooth)
## KernSmooth 2.23 loaded
## Copyright M. P. Wand 1997-2009
# Configuration
T <- 1000
t <- (1:T)/T

n <- 100
x <- (1:n)/n
rsnr <- 5

# Define the 4 true functions
truef1 <- 0.5 + (0.2*cos(4*pi*t)) + (0.1*cos(24*pi*t))
truef2 <- 0.2 + 0.6*(t > 1/3 & t <= 0.75)
truef3 <- 4*sin(4*pi*t) - sign(t - 0.3) - sign(0.72 - t) + 5
truef4 <- sqrt(t*(1 - t)) * sin((2*pi*1.05)/(t + 0.05)) + 0.5

plot(t,truef1,type="l",col="red",lwd=2,main="f1")

plot(t,truef2,type="l",col="blue",lwd=2,main="f2")

plot(t,truef3,type="l",col="purple",lwd=2,main="f3")

plot(t,truef4,type="l",col="green",lwd=2,main="f4")

# Generate Y observations for f1
f1 <- 0.5 + (0.2*cos(4*pi*x)) + (0.1*cos(24*pi*x))
sigma1 <- sd(f1)/rsnr
Y1 <- f1 + rnorm(n, mean=0, sd=sigma1)
plot(x,Y1,pch=19,main="Data Y1"); lines(t,truef1,col="red",lwd=2)

# Generate Y observations for f2
f2 <- 0.2 + 0.6*(x > 1/3 & x <= 0.75)
sigma2 <- sd(f2)/rsnr
Y2 <- f2 + rnorm(n, mean=0, sd=sigma2)
plot(x,Y2,pch=19,main="Data Y2"); lines(t,truef2,col="blue",lwd=2)

# Generate Y observations for f2
f3 <- 4*sin(4*pi*x) - sign(x - .3) - sign(.72 - x) + 5
sigma3 <- sd(f3)/rsnr
Y3 <- f3 + rnorm(n, mean=0, sd=sigma3)
plot(x,Y3,pch=19,main="Data Y3"); lines(t,truef3,col="purple",lwd=2)

# Generate Y observations for f2
f4 <- sqrt(x*(1-x))*sin((2*pi*1.05)/(x+.05)) + 0.5
sigma4 <- sd(f4)/rsnr
Y4 <- f4 + rnorm(n, mean=0, sd=sigma4)
plot(x,Y4,pch=19,main="Data Y4"); lines(t,truef4,col="green",lwd=2)

From the above plots, \(f_1\) is smooth and periodic, \(f_2\) is piece-wise constant with very abrupt jumps, \(f_3\) is a mixture of oscillations and discontinuities and \(f_4\) is an oscillatory function.

Question 2

Fit a kernel estimator for each of the 4 data sets Y1 , . . . , Y4 which correspond to the functions f1 , . . . , f4 .

fit1 <- locpoly(x, Y1, bandwidth = 0.05, degree = 0)
plot(x, Y1, pch=19, col="black", main="Kernel estimate for f1")
lines(fit1, col="blue", lwd=2)
lines(t, truef1, col="orange", lwd=2, lty=2)

fit2 <- locpoly(x, Y2, bandwidth = 0.05, degree = 0)
plot(x, Y2, pch=19, col="black", main="Kernel estimate for f2")
lines(fit2, col="blue", lwd=2)
lines(t, truef2, col="orange", lwd=2, lty=2)

fit3 <- locpoly(x, Y3, bandwidth = 0.05, degree = 0)
plot(x, Y3, pch=19, col="black", main="Kernel estimate for f3")
lines(fit3, col="blue", lwd=2)
lines(t, truef3, col="orange", lwd=2, lty=2)

fit4 <- locpoly(x, Y4, bandwidth = 0.05, degree = 0)
plot(x, Y4, pch=19, col="black", main="Kernel estimate for f4")
lines(fit4, col="blue", lwd=2)
lines(t, truef4, col="orange", lwd=2, lty=2)

The Nadaraya–Watson kernel estimator provides a smooth approximation of the regression function. For smooth functions (f1), the estimate is almost accurate. For functions with discontinuities (f2, f3), smoothing introduces bias near jumps. For oscillatory functions (f4), smoothing removes fine-scale structure.

Question 3

Part I

For each regression function, vary the window parameter h for the kernel estimator.

h_values <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.2)
Y_list     <- list(Y1, Y2, Y3, Y4)
truef_list <- list(truef1, truef2, truef3, truef4)
titles     <- c("f1", "f2", "f3", "f4")

cols <- c("blue", "green", "orange")

for (k in 1:4) {

  plot(x, Y_list[[k]], pch = 19, col = "black",
       main = paste("Kernel estimation with varying h for", titles[k]),
       xlab = "x", ylab = "y")

  lines(t, truef_list[[k]], col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

  for (i in seq_along(h_values)) {
    fit <- locpoly(x, Y_list[[k]], bandwidth = h_values[i], degree = 0)
    lines(fit$x, fit$y, col = cols[i], lwd = 2)
  }

  legend("topright",
         legend = c("True f", paste("h =", h_values)),
         col = c("red", cols),
         lwd = 2, lty = c(2,1,1,1),
         cex = 0.5)

}

For all the functions, a small h like \(0.01\) tends to lower bias and increase variance, a moderate h (\(0.05\)) give a good bias-variance trade-off and a large h (\(0.2\)) over smoothes, giving low variance and high bias.

Part II

For different values of h, also plot the point squared error the point squared error \(x \mapsto (\hat f_h(x) - f(x))^2\) .

hvals <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.2)

Ylist <- list(Y1, Y2, Y3, Y4)
flist <- list(f1, f2, f3, f4)

for (j in 1:length(Ylist)) {

  Yj <- Ylist[[j]]
  fj <- flist[[j]]

  for (h in hvals) {

    fit <- locpoly(x, Yj, bandwidth = h, degree = 0, gridsize = 100)

    # pointwise squared error
    err <- (fit$y - fj)^2

    # mean squared error
    mse <- mean(err)

    plot(fit$x, err, type = "l",
         main = paste("f", j, ", h =", h),
         ylab = "Squared error",
         xlab = "x")

    # MSE value
    text(x = min(fit$x),
         y = max(err),
         labels = paste("MSE =", round(mse, 4)),
         adj = c(0, 1))
  }
}

Increasing the value of h also increases the MSE. However a very small MSE could suggest over fitting so it is better to choose a neither too small nor too large h.

Part III

What do you find about the bias and variance of the estimators as h varies ?

Answer:

As h increases, the variance of the kernel estimator decreases while its bias increases. Small bandwidths lead to noisy but close to accurate estimates, whereas large bandwidths produce smooth but biased estimates.

So for a smooth function like \(f_1\), we can use larger bandwidth without introducing much bias. For piece-wise functions like \(f_2\) and \(f_3\), a large h creates strong bias near discontinuities. We need a low bandwidth for functions like \(f_4\) to capture local variations at the cost of higher variance.

Question 4

What can you say about the quality of the choice of h by cross-validation for the estimation of the regression functions \(f_1\) , . . . , \(f_4\) ?

bw1 <- dpill(x, Y1)
bw2 <- dpill(x, Y2)
bw3 <- dpill(x, Y3)
bw4 <- dpill(x, Y4)

bw1; bw2; bw3; bw4
## [1] 0.03756561
## [1] 0.02419233
## [1] 0.02312501
## [1] 0.02322242
fits <- list(
  locpoly(x,Y1,bandwidth=bw1),
  locpoly(x,Y2,bandwidth=bw2),
  locpoly(x,Y3,bandwidth=bw3),
  locpoly(x,Y4,bandwidth=bw4)
)

truefs <- list(truef1,truef2,truef3,truef4)
Ys <- list(Y1,Y2,Y3,Y4)

for (i in 1:4) {
  plot(x, Ys[[i]], pch=19, col="black",
       main=paste("CV bandwidth for f",i))
  lines(fits[[i]], col="blue", lwd=2)
  lines(t, truefs[[i]], col="orange", lwd=2, lty=2)
}

For the smooth function \(f_1\), the bandwidth selected using cross-validation works well, resulting in a good bias-variance tradeoff. Increased bias results from the cross-validated bandwidth’s tendency to oversmooth close to discontinuities (\(f_2\) and \(f_3\)). Important structure is lost for the highly oscillatory function \(f_4\) because the chosen bandwidth is frequently too big to capture quick local fluctuations. In general, cross-validation performs rather well globally, but it has trouble with functions that have acute local features.
